Setting rate limits purely by HTTP requests per minute rather than token volume. A single request with a 100,000-token context consumes 100x more compute than a 100-token request.

cost-capacity.title: In a shared inference cluster, what causes GPU VRAM fragmentation over time, and how do memory allocators prevent out-of-memory errors?
cost-capacity.answer: In LLM serving, requests arrive with unpredictable prompt lengths and generate variable completion lengths. Standard CUDA memory allocation (cudaMalloc and cudaFree) is notoriously slow and causes external memory fragmentation: allocating and freeing variable-sized activation and KV cache tensors creates small, non-contiguous free memory gaps. Over time, total free VRAM might be 15 GB, but the largest contiguous block is only 2 GB, causing a new allocation to fail with an OutOfMemory error. Production inference engines eliminate this through two mechanisms. First, PyTorch's caching allocator maintains pools of allocated memory blocks, splitting and merging contiguous blocks without calling cudaFree. Second, modern LLM engines (like vLLM) use PagedAttention: they pre-allocate 90% of available GPU VRAM at startup into a fixed-size block pool (e.g. 16 tokens per block). KV cache is allocated as non-contiguous physical pages mapped via a virtual page table, eliminating KV cache fragmentation entirely.
tradeOffs: PagedAttention completely eliminates KV cache fragmentation and boosts throughput by 2x to 4x, but requires virtual page table lookup overhead in custom CUDA attention kernels.
Pre-allocating GPU VRAM at engine startup prevents other processes from sharing the GPU dynamically.
followUps: How does PagedAttention borrow architectural concepts from virtual memory in operating systems?
What is the difference between internal and external memory fragmentation in GPU allocators?
wrongAnswers: Calling torch.cuda.empty_cache() after every inference request. empty_cache() forces synchronization across all CUDA streams and flushes memory pools to the OS, causing massive latency spikes.
Assuming that GPU memory fragmentation is caused by model weight tensors. Model weights are static; fragmentation is driven by dynamic KV cache and activation allocations.

cost-capacity.title: How do you allow teams to burst beyond their baseline GPU quota during off-peak hours while guaranteeing zero latency degradation for production SLAs?
cost-capacity.answer: To maximize cluster utilization without buying excess hardware, clusters allow idle capacity to be consumed as burst quota. However, burst workloads must never degrade production latency SLAs. We implement a Two-Tier Priority Class and Preemption Architecture on Kubernetes or Slurm. Every node pool defines Guaranteed Capacity and Opportunistic Capacity. Production workloads run with PriorityClass 'Production-High' and declare explicit resource requests matching limits. Internal research and batch workloads run with PriorityClass 'Batch-Opportunistic'. When the cluster is idle, batch jobs scale up into spare GPUs. The moment a production request or job arrives, the scheduler immediately schedules it: if all GPUs are full, the scheduler preempts (evicts) the lowest-priority batch job, freeing the GPU. Furthermore, to prevent network and memory bus noisy-neighbor interference on co-located nodes, we use MIG or dedicated node taints to isolate production traffic from batch workloads.
tradeOffs: Opportunistic bursting increases overall cluster hardware utilization from 40% to over 85%, but batch workloads must be designed to tolerate frequent preemptions and resume from checkpoints.
Hard node isolation guarantees zero noisy-neighbor interference, but reduces the pool of shared burstable nodes.
followUps: How do Kubernetes resource requests vs limits differ when scheduling burstable GPU workloads?
How do you prevent noisy-neighbor memory bandwidth contention on multi-GPU nodes when one GPU saturates PCIe bus bandwidth?
wrongAnswers: Giving all teams the same priority class and hoping fair-share scheduling responds fast enough for sub-second production inference traffic.
Allowing burst jobs to run without preemption support, forcing production jobs to wait in queue behind multi-hour batch runs.

cost-capacity.title: How do you design an automated GPU reclamation controller that detects zombie or idle development notebooks and frees allocated VRAM?
cost-capacity.answer: In AI development clusters, data scientists frequently spin up GPU Jupyter notebooks, run experiments, and leave them idle overnight, locking expensive A100/H100 instances. We design an Automated GPU Reclamation Controller running as a Kubernetes controller daemon. The controller queries NVIDIA Data Center GPU Manager (DCGM) metrics exported to Prometheus at 60-second intervals. For each active pod, it evaluates two primary signals: 1) Average GPU compute utilization (DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL) over a rolling 30-minute window, and 2) Active CUDA kernel execution count. If compute utilization remains below 1% and no kernel runs for 30 consecutive minutes, the controller transitions the pod to 'IDLE_WARNING' state, sending an automated notification to the owner via Slack or email with a 15-minute grace period link to dismiss. If no user heartbeat is received before grace expires, the controller takes a lightweight pod snapshot, unbinds the GPU resource, and shuts down the container.
tradeOffs: Automated idle reclamation recovers 20% to 35% of wasted cluster GPU spend, but can accidentally terminate legitimately waiting interactive sessions if utilization thresholds are set too aggressively.
Measuring GPU compute utilization alone is insufficient; memory read/write activity and active CPU data loaders must be factored in to prevent killing jobs waiting on slow I/O.
followUps: Why is checking nvidia-smi memory usage alone insufficient to determine whether a notebook is idle?
How do you preserve unsaved notebook code when an idle development container is terminated?
wrongAnswers: Checking only allocated VRAM to detect idle status. PyTorch pre-allocates and holds VRAM even when completely idle, so an idle notebook will falsely appear 100% active.
Immediately killing containers without a warning notification or grace period, frustrating researchers and destroying uncheckpointed exploratory code.

cost-capacity.title: Compare Kubernetes with the NVIDIA GPU Operator against Slurm for managing large-scale multi-tenant AI training clusters.
cost-capacity.answer: Slurm and Kubernetes originate from different paradigms. Slurm was purpose-built for High-Performance Computing (HPC) and tightly coupled MPI/NCCL multi-node batch training. It natively supports gang-scheduling (all-or-nothing scheduling of hundreds of nodes), topology-aware placement (allocating GPUs on the same InfiniBand leaf switches to minimize network hops), and low-overhead job queues with advanced fair-share algorithms. However, Slurm lacks native microservices support, container-native CI/CD, and dynamic API autoscaling. Kubernetes is the industry standard for cloud-native microservices, continuous serving, and heterogeneous infrastructure. With the NVIDIA GPU Operator, it manages driver installation, device plugins, and monitoring. However, standard Kubernetes kube-scheduler lacks native batch gang-scheduling and fair-share queuing; supporting large training clusters requires adding specialized open-source schedulers like Volcano or Kueue. In production, enterprises often run Slurm for multi-thousand GPU foundational pre-training clusters, and Kubernetes for fine-tuning, inference serving, and end-to-end AI applications.
tradeOffs: Slurm offers superior network-topology-aware job placement and minimal scheduling latency for monolithic distributed pre-training runs.
Kubernetes provides a unified control plane for inference serving, web APIs, vector databases, and MLOps pipelines under a single ecosystem.
followUps: What is topology-aware scheduling, and why does placement across InfiniBand leaf switches impact AllReduce speed?
How does Kueue bring batch scheduling capabilities to standard Kubernetes clusters?
wrongAnswers: Claiming that standard default Kubernetes can handle large-scale distributed training out of the box without specialized batch schedulers. Without gang-scheduling, default Kubernetes schedules partial pods and deadlocks.
Assuming Slurm can easily run dynamic, auto-scaling real-time web microservices with ingress routing.
